chapter: Second European tour and the crash
title: Nazi pressure voids his Haus Germania contract
summary: He explains that his Berlin birthday-gift contract was barred because the rising Nazi Party did not want American or Black music.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Europe had sort of lost the spark. And what made me lose the spark was, when I was in the (HAUS GERMANIA), the year before, for my birthday, which was in June, the fellow gave me three months to return to the following year, next year. To come back there, that was my birthday present, see? And the (HAUS GERMANIA), that was in Scharlottenburg, that was a wonderful place. Where they even -- the roof opened up and the stage came up from the floor, you see? Oh, it was a real, real modern cabaret.
And also, meanwhile, (Duisberg), my manager, Eddie (Duisberg), he had procured six months in London at the Savoy Hotel. That made nine months of the following year was already taken up.

See, but what happened was that when they Hitler party began to rear its head and old man von Hindenburg was becoming old and incompetent, see, of handling the government, you see, Hitler was not in power, but he was practically, in the he was making the power. Well, the first thing, they didn't want any American music -- the Nazi Party, they didn't want any American music, and especially the ragtime or jazz played by blacks. They didn't honor blacks at all. So, they refused, they barred the contract, they discredited the contract, and I couldn't use it.
